 Rubio says no evidence recent tech outages are linked or ‘nefarious’ 







MANILA, Philippines (AFP)—United States (US) authorities have found “zero evidence” that recent outages across tech platforms are related to one another or due to the work of “nefarious actors,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday.

The top American diplomat’s comments, on the sidelines of a Southeast Asian summit, follow multiple disruptions of everything from US air traffic operations to a Microsoft email and messaging breakdown, banking and mobile pay problems and the outage of a top-secret US government communications network.

“The first thing I want to make very clear is that we have zero evidence whatsoever — we have no indication, no evidence, and no reason to believe at all that any of these incidents are related to each other,” Rubio told reporters in Manila while on a trip to Asia with US President Donald Trump.

“The second is that we have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind.”

Rubio took time out of his diplomatic schedule in a bid to to soothe jitters back home, where thousands of Americans saw their flights grounded, along with outages in banking and communications.

Earlier Tuesday a top-secret network that the National Security Agency uses for internal communications went down, the agency acknowledged.

The NSA said it had experienced “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” but that its capabilities remained operational and “our ability to defend national security continues.”

The Trump administration has insisted Americans and their various systems remain secure, with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin insisting that the wave of recent outages does not stem from cyber criminals.

“I can tell you with complete certainty that we are not under attack,” Mullin told CNBC. “There’s no cyber threat that’s taking place. The homeland is very secure.”

 US loses measles-free status as cases, deaths mount 







WASHINGTON, United States (AFP)—The United States has lost its long-held status of having eradicated measles, as declining vaccination rates have seen cases of the dangerous and highly contagious virus soar around the country, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced Tuesday.

Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their elimination statuses, PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa told a virtual press briefing, while Guatemala is at risk of losing its designation following its own major spike in cases this year.

The outbreak in the United States — its worst in over three decades, with more than 5,400 cases reported this year — has prompted criticism of the Trump administration’s handling of the crisis.

Medical experts have accused US President Donald Trump and his health secretary, noted vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr, of fanning distrust in vaccinations by repeatedly highlighting unfounded safety concerns.

The vast majority of cases have occurred among people who had not been vaccinated. At least 12 deaths have been reported since 2025 — when the disease came roaring back — mainly in young children.

Kennedy on Tuesday vowed to “stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain US measles elimination status.”

“I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” he wrote on X, referring to measles, mumps and rubella.

Trump notably signed an executive order, alongside Kennedy, earlier this year calling for the combination MMR vaccine — the standard in the United States — to be separated into individual shots, a move broadly opposed by physician groups as unnecessary and dangerous for public health.

“It’s shameful, it’s sad, it’s scandalous,” Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the US House of Representatives, told reporters Tuesday of the elimination status being rescinded.

“It’s a direct result of the policies that have been pursued by the secretary of Health and Human Services (Kennedy): the vaccine denial, the failure to rely on science, and the fact that communities across the country…have been put into harm’s way.”

Measles elimination status does not mean there are no cases at all, but rather there has been no sustained spread of the virus for over a year.

– ‘Year after year’ –

“For more than a generation, the United States kept measles at bay by vaccinating children, tracking the disease and responding quickly when cases emerged,” said American Academy of Pediatrics President Andrew Racine, adding that the disease’s reemergence is a “preventable failure to protect children.”

Canada has shown progress in attacking its outbreak, with two consecutive months of no new cases, PAHO director Barbosa said, noting the trend must continue for a full year to regain its status.

Measles causes fever, respiratory symptoms and a rash, and in some cases more serious complications such as pneumonia and brain inflammation, which can lead to severe long-term health problems or even death.

The virus is transmitted through the air and is extremely contagious, remaining airborne for up to two hours after an infected person has left the area.

To curb its spread, experts say that the vaccination rate must hit at least 95 percent of the population. However, in the United States, the vaccination rate among kindergarten students was below 93 percent in 2025, with much lower rates in various local areas, especially among some conservative religious communities.

Several of the deaths in Pennsylvania and one death in New York have reportedly occurred among the Amish community.

Before the vaccine was developed in the early 1960s, measles killed hundreds of children each year across the US. It continues to claim tens of thousands of lives worldwide.

Paul Offit, an American pediatrician specializing in infectious diseases, warned ahead of the PAHO’s official announcement that measles cases would continue to spread unless vaccination rates return to higher levels.

“It’s going to be back next year and the year after that. And until we get immunization rates up, it’s going to continue to be back,” he told AFP.

 International News, Latest News 

November 17, 2026




 US Democrats take step toward first Black House speaker 







WASHINGTON (AFP), United States—Hakeem Jeffries is set to move closer Wednesday to becoming the first Black speaker of the US House of Representatives as Democrats prepare to choose their leader following a landslide midterm election victory.

The 56-year-old New Yorker faces no declared challenger in a closed-door party election, but opposition from some newly elected progressives has exposed divisions over how Democrats should use their newfound power.

Jeffries is poised to preside over a commanding Democratic majority during the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term, with his party seeking to reverse the Republican president’s policies and hold his administration to account.

He said Tuesday he would request a recorded vote on his nomination, departing from the wishes of some allies who had hoped he would be chosen “by acclamation” — without a formal ballot.

Jeffries told reporters at the Capitol on the eve of the ballot that every Democrat should have the opportunity to weigh his experience, record and vision, citing the precedent set when the party last won control of the House in 2018.

Wednesday’s vote will select the party’s nominee for speaker, but Jeffries must still win a formal election of the full House when the new Congress convenes on January 3.

Both returning Democrats and incoming lawmakers can participate in Wednesday’s nomination, including progressives who have sought concessions from Jeffries on issues ranging from US military support for Israel to the influence of money in politics.

Some have threatened to withhold their votes, although the dissent has not produced a rival candidate.

Jeffries and his allies have been working to consolidate support, meeting with newly elected lawmakers and reassuring different factions that their voices will be heard.

The Democratic leader has also sought to shift attention to the party’s plans for governing after voters handed Republicans a crushing defeat amid anger over the Iran war and soaring fuel costs.

“Folks are drowning in this Republican economy, and House Democrats are committed to turning that situation around, beginning on day one,” he told reporters Tuesday.

“We’re going to relentlessly fight for an affordable America.”

– Brooklyn roots –

Raised in Brooklyn’s Crown Heights neighborhood, Jeffries trained as a lawyer before entering the New York state legislature in 2007 and winning election to Congress in 2012.

Known for his measured manner, sharp rhetoric and penchant for quoting hip-hop artists, he became the first Black politician to lead a party in either chamber of Congress when Democrats chose him to succeed Nancy Pelosi in 2022.

He also served as a House prosecutor during Trump’s first impeachment trial in 2020.

His expected elevation would represent a landmark in American politics, putting him in charge of one of Washington’s most powerful institutions and second in line to the presidency behind the vice president.

But Jeffries would inherit a formidable task in managing a Democratic coalition spanning centrists and an increasingly assertive left flank.

His party has promised investigations into Trump and his administration, while lawmakers remain divided over Israel, healthcare and how aggressively to pursue their agenda against a president who retains veto power.

The relatively straightforward House leadership election contrasts with a more competitive contest among Senate Democrats, where veteran leader Chuck Schumer faces a challenge from progressive Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen.

Van Hollen has attracted support from prominent left-wing figures, including Bernie Sanders, but acknowledges he is the underdog. Senate Democrats will elect their leader in early December.

Republicans chose their own congressional leaders last week, elevating Trump ally Jim Jordan in the House and retaining John Thune in the Senate.

news.title: Democrats notch another win in midterm Senate race, bag Alaska seat
news.text: Digital Desk | New York, Nov 18 (IANS) The Democrats' blue wave swept the contentious Alaska Senate seat to their ranks, with Mary Peltola declared the winner. The last Senate result to be announced, it raised on Tuesday the Democratic Party's tally to 56 in the 100-member Senate, flipping nine Republican seats. After the media announced her victory, Peltola said on X, "There is no greater honour than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first". Peltola, who squeaked past the 50 per cent threshold by 0.12 per cent, defeated the sitting Republican Senator Dan S Sullivan in the state that President Donald Trump had carried by 13 per cent. The Democrats had been accused of putting up a candidate with a name similar to Sullivan, except for a middle initial, to confuse the voters. President Donald Trump had said that the second Sullivan's votes went to the Republicans. Since Peltola had won more than 50 per cent of the votes, it won't make a difference, and there will be no need for a run-off by the two top contenders either, as Alaska requires one if none of the candidates gets more than half the votes polled. The Justice Department tried unsuccessfully in a federal court to block the official declaration of the results if she is elected, citing the second Dan. Peltola will be the first Native American from Alaska to serve in the Senate. She was by trade a commercial fisher, and her election slogan was 4Fs -- "Fish, Family, Freedom". Fishing is important to Native Alaskans in the frigid state, a large part of which is within the Arctic Circle. The vastness of the state delayed the counting of votes. Peltola was a member of the House of Representatives but was defeated in 2024 by a Republican on the back of Trump's victory.

news.title: 'Business as usual': Nvidia's Kress passes first test as board slams door on Huang
news.text: SAN FRANCISCO: Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress expressed confidence in the chipmaker's business, leadership and staff and pledged to be "disciplined in how we commit capital," seeking to reassure investors on the first earnings call since its co-founder Jensen Huang quit. She took the helm last week following news that Huang had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom US intelligence agencies are investigating over her ties to the Chinese government, revelations that have knocked more than $700 billion off Nvidia's market value. Kress initially stumbled as she read out prepared remarks but gained resolve as the call progressed on Tuesday. "Our leadership has stood up so strongly over the last week," she said, ⁠responding to an analyst's question about what could change during the leadership transition. "From a business perspective, it's business as usual." Management had engaged with Nvidia's suppliers and partners, who were backing the company to the hilt, she said, with key contractor TSMC visiting Nvidia's offices this week. Nvidia shares rose more than 4% in extended trading, after it forecast fourth-quarter revenue above Wall Street estimates and fiscal 2028 sales to grow about 75% year over year. "Nvidia showed the AI story can be bigger than Jensen Huang," said Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, New York. "The strength of the business and underlying demand gave traders reason to believe the story can keep moving forward without him at the helm." Loyal employees and big tech allies, including Elon Musk, have called for Huang's reinstatement. US President Donald Trump has also backed him. Huang, who was the face of the company that has underpinned the AI boom with its cutting-edge chips, said on Tuesday he would be "honored" to be Nvidia's CEO again. But new board Chairman Harvey Jones rejected the idea, saying on the post-earnings call: "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted (Huang's) resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Succession in focus Nvidia kept the post-earnings call shorter than usual - around 50 minutes, versus roughly an hour in the past two quarters, when Huang led the call and answered questions more expansively. "Kress faced an unusually unforgiving debut, with every pause and phrase being ⁠scrutinised. It should not define her ability to lead," said PP Foresight analyst Paolo Pescatore. "The more meaningful test is her command of the business, how she handles difficult questions and the confidence she builds around the decisions ahead." Kress is known to have stood up to Huang's risky, multibillion-dollar financing deals that have fuelled concerns of a circular AI economy. She ⁠was joined on the call by ⁠Ian Buck, the vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, whom some analysts view as a top CEO candidate. However, he did not speak on the call. "Buck’s appearance will inevitably be viewed as an informal audition ... but his participation alone should not be read as a signal that the board has chosen ⁠its next CEO," Pescatore said. Neocloud policy spelled out Investors have been concerned that without Huang, Nvidia could pull back investments in debt-laden neoclouds, which rely partly on Nvidia's backing to fund their data center buildouts, an issue the company sought to address in its CFO commentary on its website. Neocloud investments as of the end of the third quarter fell to $32 billion from $36 billion in the prior quarter. The company said its neocloud commitments would kick in only once partners secured financing and their capacity was operational, and could be cut or scrapped if that did not happen in time. Asked on the call whether the disclosure language on neocloud investments reflected a change in how Nvidia deals with them, Kress said: "Is it new? No. Did we change anything? No. "What this is only saying is that we wanted to make sure ... it was very clear as we had been receiving some questions on how that exactly worked." This week was "a referendum on AI," Direxion's Behan said, with Nvidia's results testing spending on AI infrastructure and Anthropic's upcoming market debut testing how much investors are willing to pay for companies trying to profit from it. "We've got this," Kress said, as she ended the call. )

news.text: Having been jailed for 10 years and six months, disgraced entertainer Russell Brand remains very much in the headlines. Since his conviction, six more women have come forward with allegations of misconduct. Meanwhile, Brand’s voice and image continue to be broadcast around the world, and not just in the form of news stories and documentaries. Brand’s X account remains open, and his popular YouTube channel recently uploaded a pre-recorded episode of his Sunday Service programme that also featured a post-sentencing letter penned by Brand and read aloud by his wife, Laura Gallacher. news.title: Trump unveils his new plan to renovate the White House
news.text:
US president Donald Trump is launching new plans to renovate the White House grounds, despite voter criticism that he is focusing too much on personal projects.

His administration is spending around $3m (€2.7m) to replace the stones in Lafayette Square as part of the president’s overhaul of the public park across the street from the White House, according to documents seen by The Washington Post.

The US National Park Service will pay for the work, officials told the newspaper, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Another project is under way to expand a black granite walkway that Mr Trump installed outside the West Wing earlier this year. The new walkway would stretch past the Rose Garden to a roadway south of the White House.

The latest plans come after voters delivered a stinging rebuke to Mr Trump’s Republicans in the mid-term elections earlier this month.

Voters’ major focus was the cost of living, while corruption was raised as a leading concern, adding to criticism that Mr Trump had prioritised personal projects and grandiose construction plans over the issues affecting ordinary Americans.

The president has defended his decisions, lashing out at a reporter on Monday who cited opponents questioning whether his focus on the projects was distracting from other priorities. He told her: “You never noticed the broken windows, obviously”, then praised the new helipad and planned ballroom.

“It takes me 10 minutes a day, very little time… 10 minutes a day [to work on White House construction projects],” Mr Trump said Monday.

“Losers like you come out and they say, ‘Why are you focused on the White House?’ Because the White House is a symbol of our country.”

His comments drew accusations of racism, after he also told the reporter, Yamiche Alcindor, a black Haitian-American who works for NBC News, that she had “never noticed broken windows” and did not “see dirt”.

“You never noticed broken windows, obviously, from where you come,” he said.

Mr Trump claimed that he was paying for the White House projects, although he did not specify which ones.

“This is peanuts. And I pay for it. This doesn’t cost money,” Mr Trump said. “This is called talent, talent. You don’t have talent. You don’t know what a broke column is.”

news.title: MAHA Rejoices After White House Drops Controversial FDA Nomination
news.text:
The Trump administration pulled its nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), setting off a dispute over whether Senate Republicans or the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement forced her out.

Heidi Overton, a physician and deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, will now be replaced by another nominee as the White House seeks to advance its MAHA agenda, according to Axios.

“FDA nominee Heidi Overton lacks the support on the Hill to move forward with her confirmation,” a senior administration official told Axios late Tuesday.

“We need to go in a new direction at FDA, and everybody fully supports [Health] Secretary Kennedy’s vision to Make America Healthy Again and get back to a more populist and common-sense approach to health in America,” the official added, according to Axios.

Scoop: White House drops Heidi Overton’s FDA nomination https://t.co/CYriTACwk2— Axios (@axios) November 18, 2026

The White House’s move came at the last moment as the Senate health committee was due to vote on Overton’s nomination Wednesday, the New York Times reported. 

Nominated by President Donald Trump in August, Overton underwent a Senate confirmation hearing in September. She had already drawn opposition from Democrats, some Republicans and some MAHA activists.

Republican Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy, the chair of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP), had expressed “strong concerns” about the nomination back in August. Overton, he wrote, lacked the managerial experience required at an organization as large and beleaguered as the FDA. 

“Additionally, Dr. Overton’s active role in last week’s nonsensical vaccine executive order calls into question her commitment to standing up for sound science and protecting children’s health. That alone is almost disqualifying,” he added.

Cassidy responded to the withdrawal by saying that Overton still had a “viable” path to confirmation. 

“Tonight, the White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton. The WH said that this was because she did not have the votes to pass. This was odd as I was having productive conversations with members. I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate.”

Overton helped draft and edit the scientific justification for revising the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC) childhood vaccine recommendations from 18 to 11—a justification that would inform President Trump’s executive order on childhood vaccinations, Semafor reported. 

While a former senior administration official told Semafor that Overton drove the policy push, which was supported by Health Secretary and MAHA advocate Robert F. Kennedy Jr., another senior administration official said the push reflected the White House’s “top-down” approach and not Overton’s personal ideas.

Some influential MAHA advocates also questioned Overton’s nomination, alleging that she would side with health and agriculture interests and help undermine the MAHA agenda, according to Axios. (RELATED: EXCLUSIVE: Big Pharma Insider Backing RFK Jr.’s Pick To Lead FDA)

Alex Voetberg, née Clark, a prominent MAHA advocate, dismissed mainstream media reports that the withdrawal of Overton’s nomination had anything to do with Senate Republicans’ concerns, writing, “The explanation they’re looking for is the power of MAHA activists.” 

“It’s remarkable how quickly the atmosphere in Washington can change. Susie Wiles is out. Stephen Miller is in. And almost immediately, we’re seeing movement on issues that MAGA and MAHA voters have been demanding action on for TWO YEARS. Now even Heidi Overton’s out for FDA,” she added. 

Some pro-life advocates reportedly also doubted that Overton would tighten rules for prescribing the abortion pill mifepristone.

“This narrative took hold that Heidi was not aligned with Kennedy on this, was more aligned with pharma [on] vaccine stuff, and was in favor of a more maximal vaccine schedule,” the former senior administration official told Semafor. “And that’s just not the case, not what happened.”

news.title: Trump calls Venezuela a US ‘acquisition’, pitches energy partnership to Philippines
news.text:
President Donald Trump referred to Venezuela as an “acquisition” while touting an increasing supply of US energy he said will benefit American allies including the Philippines.

“We have more energy than any country in the world,” Trump said during a meeting in Manila with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. Wednesday. “If you add Russia and Saudi Arabia together, we’re much bigger than those two combined. And then you add Venezuela — which was our new acquisition.”

“It was an acquisition, whether people like to say that or not,” Trump said of Venezuela. He said the war or “whatever it may be” with the South American nation lasted 48 minutes, referring to the US operation in January to depose former Venezuelan strongman Nicolás Maduro.

US plans to expand Venezuelan oil output

Under an agreement reached after Maduro’s ouster, the US attained a majority control of a large amount of Venezuela’s oil wealth. North American Blue Energy Partners, the US government-backed producer of Venezuelan oil, plans to more than double crude output in just over two years.

Alaska pipeline and nuclear energy cooperation

The US president also hailed plans for “a major new pipeline in Alaska to export affordable, abundant supplies of energy to our allies and friends across the Pacific. And the Philippines would be a very natural partner in this effort.”

Trump additionally pointed to collaboration with Manila on nuclear energy. “For the Philippines to embrace American technology in its first modern nuclear project would underscore the strength of the important relationship, and we’re going to probably do something very big having to do with nuclear,” the US president said.

Philippines faces pressure on domestic gas supplies

The Philippines, a longstanding treaty ally of the US, faces major pressure from the depletion of its main Malampaya gas field, which has fueled a fifth of its power plants. In 2023, the nation began importing liquefied natural gas for the first time as production at its main Malampaya gas field dwindled.

news.title: Trump Says US Rare Earths Production Will Match China’s Within 10 Months
news.text:
The United States should have enough rare earth minerals within 10 months to supply its own critical materials needed for national security, energy, and industry, President Donald Trump said on Nov. 17.

Reaching the milestone would allow the United States to loosen China’s grip on the world’s supply of materials and minerals, and ensure its own supply chain, although one expert called the timeframe “unrealistic.”

“We are making rare earths at a level that we’ve never made before. …We’re gonna catch them within 10 months, they say,” Trump told reporters in Manila during the first day of a three-day trip to Asia.

The president made the remarks to reporters during a photo session with Prime Minister of India Narendra Modi, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. They were gathered for a QUAD (Quadrilateral Security Dialogue) leaders meeting on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) conference.

Trump didn’t provide details but said the United States was working on projects over the next 12 months and had made several new critical mineral deals to secure supply chains independent of China.

“These will make our countries much stronger and, at the same time, guarantee safety,” Trump told leaders later during a roundtable discussion. “We’re working very closely on minerals, rare earths, and everything else. We have a lot of things happening over the next 12 months that will very much surprise people.”

China has dominated the global processing and supply of rare earth elements for the past 60 years as a result of strategic planning aided by cheap capital and lax environmental regulations.

The country also manufactures about 95 percent of the global supply of permanent rare earth magnets needed for electric vehicles, wind turbines, and defense systems.

“Everything that we need we’ll have in 10 months,” Trump said. “We’re producing major numbers when it comes to rare earths. And [Japan and India are] too, by the way. We’re all doing it.”

For decades, the United States and its allies had stopped mining and outsourced manufacturing of its critical minerals, without due consideration for threats to the supply chain posed by communist China.

Meanwhile, Beijing has poured resources into rare earth mining and processing across the globe, consolidating it under Communist Party control.

China also has control over heavy rare earths including terbium, graphite processing, and cobalt refining, according to the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA).

Jack Lifton, co-chairman of the Toronto-based think tank Critical Minerals Institute, warned that the United States’s needs to direct effort not only into rare earth supply but also manufacturing capability.

“China’s rare earth industry did not become dominant merely because its government financed mineral deposits or announced manufacturing capacity,” he said in a note Tuesday. “It developed an increasingly integrated industrial system, accumulated manufacturing experience, expanded production, and established relationships with customers. Whatever one thinks of China’s industrial policies, the resulting manufacturing capabilities are real.

“The United States cannot reproduce in a few years, through financial commitments alone, an industrial system that took decades to develop,” Lifton added.

The Trump administration has invested in and helped several new mining and production projects get started in allied countries and in the United States.

In August, Trump held a roundtable with the mining industry where he announced over $2 billion in additional critical mining and mining-related projects.

The Department of War is investing over $85 million into Strategic Bauxite to secure a supply of refractory-grade bauxite to support manufacturing of high-temperature-resistant materials to make components for the military, Trump said.

The department was also investing $150 million into Niron Magnetics in Minnesota to produce permanent magnets, free of rare earth metals, to support the defense industrial base.

Other investments the administration was making included $400 million into a full scandium value chain, and the first scandium mine for a supply chain of high-heat aluminum alloys for fighter jets and spacecraft.

The Export-Import Bank was investing in a boron deposit in California, graphite in Alabama, and tantalum and niobium in Pennsylvania.

The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation was spending $4.8 million to develop a rare earth mine in Madagascar to secure magnet metals.

The Energy Department was investing $100 million in 14 mining schools to train the next generation in mining, minerals, and supply chains.

Rep. Mark Alford (R-Mo.), said he helped his state secure up to $160 million in federal funding for critical mineral projects.

“Missouri contains 36 of the 60 federally designated critical minerals, and I’m proud to have helped secure up to $160 million in federal funding to put them to work through a new initiative in Kansas City!” he posted on X Nov. 17.
news.summary: One expert doubted the president's timeline, saying China took decades to achieve dominance over the industry.
news.author: Jill McLaughlin

news.title: Stumped CNN Host Sounds Alarm on Mystery Outage Hell
news.text:
Erin Burnett is sounding the alarm over America’s string of unexplained outages and President Donald Trump’s failure to address them, as well as the failure of his close allies. 

Burnett, 50, opened Tuesday’s OutFront with news that NSA Net, the spy agency’s classified internal communications system, had been offline for upward of eight hours. According to CNN sources, there is no concrete sign of a cyberattack. 

“But like every other of these outages in recent days, it is unclear as to... if not that, then what?” Burnett asked. 

The NSA chalked it up to “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.” A spokesperson insisted that “mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational.” 

However, Burnett noted this is just the latest in a run of failures that began last week, hitting Microsoft, the FAA, Workday, Chase and United. Apple joined the list on Tuesday, with glitches both online and in its stores. Apple took partial responsibility, telling OutFront, “an internal update caused some outages this morning.”

The issue is so widespread that Burnett highlighted how lawmakers, both Democrats and Republicans, have joined forces.

Burnett then played clips of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Republican Sen. Josh Hawley. Jeffries called the developments “troubling,” while Hawley scoffed: “If this is all a coincidence, it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.”

“There is not a lot that Hakeem Jeffries and Josh Hawley agree on, and they are completely copacetic on that one,” Burnett noted.

The CNN host then highlighted other notable names calling out the outages.

Sen. Rick Scott, for instance, posted on X that Americans “feel like they’re not getting the whole story.”

Burnett pointed the finger at Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, 55, for his lack of understanding of the outages four days later, before taking aim at the president.

“The root cause of what happened, we don’t have clarity yet,” Duffy said during a press conference on Tuesday in a clip Burnett aired. “If we were subject to a hack, we will share that with you as well. But all of my intelligence partners are telling me that wasn’t the case.” 

Duffy has also pinned the ground stop on contractor L3Harris, which was swapping out old copper lines for fiber at an FAA site in El Dorado, Arkansas. 

The Washington Post reported that on Tuesday, he took a shot at the company, claiming they should “hire better minds.” 

Burnett ran through a string of online reactions. Former Trump White House Press Secretary Sean Spicer declared on X, “I’m entering full prepper mode.”

Conservative radio host Todd Starnes, 59, sparked concerns over a possible bank run, while journalist Maria Shriver, 71, leaned into the hacking conspiracy, posting it was “hard to believe this isn’t all somehow connected.” 

Meanwhile, former New York Times cyber reporter Nicole Perlroth predicted “a period of cascading failures,” adding: “This, I’m sorry to say, is just the opening chapter.”

Then came the commander in chief, with Burnett playing Trump’s answer in Manila when a reporter asked whether he was concerned about the outages. 

She suggested the president appeared to “be shrugging it off.”

“It’s life when you’re big and powerful, and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine,” Trump said flippantly.

“So having your bank account attacked just because you live in America is life. And it’s fine,” Burnett said. “Obviously not inspiring confidence.”

So far, the companies hit are taking some responsibility. Microsoft said a hidden flaw, a spike in traffic, and reduced server capacity crashed Outlook and Teams. JPMorgan Chase blamed a software bug that rippled through the financial system. 

The White House, Department of Transportation, the Department of Homeland Security, and the NSA did not immediately respond to the Daily Beast’s request for comment. White House Communications Director Steven Cheung has previously told the Daily Beast that Burnett is “a racist and a r----d.”

After taking shots at Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Vice President JD Vance’s responses to the outages, Burnett ended her monologue with a jab at Duffy, pointing to a technical glitch during a Saturday press conference at the Department of Transportation’s headquarters in Washington.

Partway through his remarks, Duffy’s microphone gave out. “Oh, wait a second here. I don’t know what’s going on with our audio,” he said.

CNNErin Burnett is sounding the alarm over America’s string of unexplained outages and President Donald Trump’s failure to address them, as well as the failure of his close allies. 

Burnett, 50, opened Tuesday’s OutFront with news that NSA Net, the spy agency’s classified internal communications system, had been offline for upward of eight hours. According to CNN sources, there is no concrete sign of a cyberattack. 

“But like every other of these outages in recent days, it is unclear as to... if not that, then what?” Burnett asked.

news.title: Nvidia rules out Huang’s return as CEO, reports revenue surge
news.text:
US chip giant Nvidia on Tuesday ruled out any comeback for ousted CEO Jensen Huang, who was forced out in a spy scandal, and reported that it had doubled revenue in the third quarter to more than $115 billion, beating expectations.

Huang sought reinstatement despite resigning last week over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, but his successor—interim CEO Colette Kress—said it was now “business as usual” as the company charts a path forward without him.

Harvey Jones, the chair of the company’s board, said in an earnings call that “the Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

Investors scoured the upbeat results for evidence that the artificial intelligence boom can withstand the Nvidia crisis, which highlighted a loophole allegedly exploited by Chinese companies.

“Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” Kress said in her first remarks since being appointed by the board last week.

She forecast stronger revenue growth of 75 per cent in the next fiscal year, up from 70 per cent.

Huang’s bid on Tuesday to get his job back was the latest twist for the company at the centre of an AI boom that has propelled markets to record highs and boosted global economic growth.

The recent upheaval has battered Nvidia shares—which have lost $700 billion in market value since the scandal broke—and Huang is to be questioned by US lawmakers on December 1 over national security concerns.

A charismatic promoter of AI, his fall triggered immediate calls from Elon Musk and others for his return, and even President Donald Trump said he “would not mind” seeing Huang back at Nvidia, downplaying the espionage allegations.

• Battle over AI chips –

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said, hours before the earnings release. 

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

As the spy scandal deepened, Washington on Monday announced new restrictions on AI chip exports, drawing condemnation from Beijing.

The new US export curbs and the wider Nvidia scandal risk casting a shadow over talks between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which starts this week in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

Under Washington’s new rules, data centres anywhere in the world will need a US license to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes.

The rules also require licenses to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil — countries the US Commerce Department says present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of the chips.

The changes are a response to a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centres in Southeast Asia and elsewhere that run on US hardware not available for export to China.

While the loophole has been known to authorities, the revelation of Huang’s affair has drawn intense scrutiny to the practice.

His lover Alice Huang, who is not related to the 63-year-old, is a former executive of Megaspeed — a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in circumvention of export controls.

Investors are watching for signs of whether Kress will slow Huang’s aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies.

Huang on Tuesday sounded a note of contrition in his statement, saying “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life.”

US chip giant Nvidia on Tuesday ruled out any comeback for ousted CEO Jensen Huang, who was forced out in a spy scandal, and reported that it had doubled revenue in the third quarter to more than $115 billion, beating expectations.

news.title: No evidence of coordinated cyberattack behind US outages – Rubio
news.text:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed fears that the country is under a coordinated cyberattack following a series of technology disruptions affecting government agencies, banks, airlines and major technology companies.

Rubio said there was no evidence linking the incidents or suggesting that they were orchestrated by hackers, criminals, foreign governments or other hostile actors.

“We are not under systemic attack,” Rubio told reporters in Manila, Philippines, on Tuesday, November 17, while travelling with President Donald Trump.

According to Reuters, Rubio acknowledged that the disruptions were unsettling but insisted that they were unrelated and had different technical causes.

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyberhackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind,” he said.

He added, “Each of them are distinct, and they’re different in their causation.”

The remarks followed a series of disruptions affecting Microsoft’s email services, United States air traffic control, major banks, United Airlines, Apple services and the National Security Agency’s internal communications network.

The Federal Aviation Administration had ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday, November 13, which lasted approximately four and a half hours, disrupting air travel across the country.

The disruption followed a Microsoft outage affecting services including Outlook and Teams, while JPMorgan Chase experienced a software problem that affected some banking services on Monday.

United Airlines also reported a technology failure that delayed approximately 150 flights.

On Tuesday, the NSA disclosed that its network had experienced a temporary disruption during scheduled maintenance, although it maintained that its mission-critical capabilities remained operational.

The agency said its ability to defend national security had continued despite the technical problems.

Intelligence chief backs Rubio

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also dismissed suggestions that the disruptions were the result of a cyberattack or state-sponsored activity.

Speaking during an interview with CNBC on Tuesday, Clayton said, “This is not a cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation-state.”

He added, “We’ve looked very closely. Anytime we see something like this, those are the first questions that we ask on behalf of the American people.”

Clayton attributed some of the problems to technology upgrades and security patches introduced to address vulnerabilities in computer systems.

“As you patch and upgrade your systems, taking them down and bringing them back up, there are things like this that happen,” he said.

He also explained that artificial intelligence was enabling organisations to identify vulnerabilities more quickly, creating pressure to upgrade and secure their systems.

Concerns persist over repeated outages

Despite the administration’s assurances, the frequency of the disruptions has prompted questions from lawmakers and some supporters of Trump.

Republican Senator Josh Hawley expressed reservations about the incidents occurring within a short period.

“If this is all a coincidence, it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world,” he told reporters.

Democratic Senator Mark Warner, vice-chairman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, also said there was no indication that the incidents were the result of a coordinated attack.

However, he called attention to the pressure artificial intelligence was placing on technology companies and government agencies to identify and fix vulnerabilities.

In a statement, Warner said, “I understand why Americans are concerned about the widespread outages we’ve seen in recent days, affecting everything from banks and major technology companies to critical government systems.”

He added, “At this point, there is no indication that these incidents are the result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort.”

Meanwhile, Trump also played down concerns over the disruptions, saying that technical problems could occur even in large and well-funded organisations.

“It’s like when you’re big and powerful, and you have all the money. Things like that happen. It’s fine,” he told reporters in Manila.

The incidents have renewed scrutiny of the reliability of critical technology infrastructure in the United States, particularly as government agencies and private companies increasingly depend on interconnected digital systems.
news.summary:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed fears that the country is under a coordinated cyberattack following a series of technology disruptions affecting government agencies, banks, airlines and major technology companies.

news.title: US lawmakers demand federal probe into Diwali event disruption in Seattle

news.title: We need Reykjavik 2.0
news.text:
Excitement abounds around the possible, perhaps likely, upcoming tripartite meeting in Shenzen, China among Presidents Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump at the November 18-19 meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Some are calling it Yalta 2.0. We’d rather think of it as Reykjavik 2.0., while also welcoming some of the broader diplomatic breakthroughs and global reordering achieved at Yalta almost 82 years ago.

 Dmitry Trenin, former longtime director of the Carnegie Moscow Center and current President of the Russian International Affairs Council, wrote encouragingly, “The US president has mentioned that an unprecedented trilateral meeting…would make sense if it were focused on denuclearization.” Trenin wrote this in Al Jazeera in the context of explaining why Russia could play a helpful role in negotiating a new nuclear agreement between its Iranian ally and the United States. While anything that might help end the dangerous, destructive, and potentially apocalyptic conflagration in Southwest Asia would be more than welcome, we think the leaders can and should reach even higher. Why not rekindle the spirit of the 1986 meeting between Presidents Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev, at which they came within a hairsbreadth, arguably one word, of eliminating not only all ballistic missiles as Reagan originally proposed but all nuclear weapons as Gorbachev countered. Reagan replied, “Yes, all” and Secretary of State George Shultz agreed. “Let’s do it,” he said. The chance to achieve the most extraordinary diplomatic breakthrough in history slipped through Reagan’s grasp when he insisted on unlimited testing of his Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) fantasy rather than limiting SDI to the laboratory for ten years. The world’s hopes were dashed and we have not come even close ever since.

 Sure, we’re up against obstacles and the odds against this are long. Donald Trump has responded to the midterm shellacking by appointing Stephen Miller as Chief of Staff—in effect giving the middle finger to those who didn’t support the Republicans, which is not a hopeful sign. Putin knows that much of Russian power comes not from its economic prowess or its conventional military but from possessing the largest nuclear arsenal in the world. And Xi Jinping has made it clear that China won’t engage in arms control talks until it achieves rough nuclear parity with the U.S. and Russia; it has been rapidly increasing the size of its arsenal as a result.

 That said, there are good reasons why all three could support this proposal. After Tuesday’s humiliating trouncing, Trump, probably the most recalcitrant of the three, may be desperate for an achievement that could cement at least a piece of a positive legacy—and in this case a very big piece, a resounding piece. And he has been all over the map on the nuclear issue. In February 2025, he said, “There’s no reason for us to be building brand-new nuclear weapons. We already have so many. You could destroy the world 50 times over, 100 times over. And here we are building new nuclear weapons, and they’re building nuclear weapons.” He also said, “We’re all spending a lot of money that we could be spending on other things that are actually, hopefully, much more productive." This is apparently something he’s been contemplating for many years. In 2016, he told the New York Times’ Maggie Haberman and David Sanger: “I personally think it’s the biggest problem the world has, nuclear capability. I think it’s the single biggest problem….Power of weaponry today is beyond anything ever thought of, or even, you know, it’s unthinkable, the power….And to me, it’s the single biggest, it’s the single biggest problem.” He credits his “very brilliant” MIT physicist uncle John Trump with making him aware of this danger.

In 1986, he sought the advice of Nobel laureate and International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War founder Dr. Bernard Lown on negotiating nuclear disarmament with Gorbachev. He told Lown that he would get Reagan to send him to Moscow and he would secure disarmament and end the Cold War in one hour.” Lown commented, “I sat there dumbfounded. ‘Who is this self-inflated individual? Is he sane or what?’”

 On January 23, 2025, he told the World Economic Forum in Davos: “And I will tell you that President Putin really liked the idea of — of cutting way back on nuclear. And I think the rest of the world, we would have gotten them to follow. And China would have come along too. China also liked it. Tremendous amounts of money are being spent on nuclear, and the destructive capability is something that we don’t even want to talk about today, because you don’t want to hear it. It’s too depressing. So, we want to see if we can denuclearize, and I think that’s very possible. And I can tell you that President Putin wanted to do it. He and I wanted to do it. We had a good conversation with China. They would have been involved, and that would have been an unbelievable thing for the planet.”

 Whether or not Trump is sane is even more heatedly debated today than it was 40 years ago, but that Trump may be iconoclastic enough to take a dramatic step that reverses the course of history should not be. The question is whether he’s capable of taking such a step in favor of humanity rather than against it.

 Similarly with Putin. Putin told a meeting of the Valdai International Discussion Club in Sochi in 2017, “Should you ask me if nuclear disarmament is possible, I will tell you ‘yes, it is possible. Does Russia wish to achieve universal nuclear disarmament or not? The answer is in the affirmative, too. Yes, it does, and it will be working for it.” Shortly before the invasion of Ukraine, the leaders of the U.S., Russia, China, France, and the United jointly declared:

"We affirm that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought... we remain committed to our Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) obligations, including our Article VI obligation to pursue negotiations in good faith on effective measures relating to cessation of the nuclear arms race at an early date and to nuclear disarmament." Skeptics will rightly point out that this was before the invasion of Ukraine and a series of slightly veiled nuclear threats that Putin issued. But it at least offers a glimmer of hope, especially in the context of a security agreement that promises peaceful coexistence for all participants.

 In 2017, in a speech at the United Nations Office in Geneva, Xi Jinping said clearly, “Nuclear weapons, the Sword of Damocles that hangs over humankind, should be completely prohibited and ultimately destroyed over time to make the world free of nuclear weapons.” While not disavowing this sentiment, Xi has more recently indicated that China would not participate in arms control discussions until it had achieved rough parity with largest nuclear powers--the United States and Russia. Fine. To most people, that means China increasing the size of its arsenal to the 5,000 plus weapons that both Russia and the United States possess. We have a different proposal. How about if the U.S. and Russia reduce their arsenals down to the 600 or so that China now possesses?

We see this being done in three four-year stages, much as Reagan and Gorbachev envisioned 40 years ago. In the first stage, the U.S. and Russia pare down their arsenals while China forgoes its expansion. During this trust-building stage, the wars in Iran and Ukraine would need to end quickly, alongside a recommitment to the UN Charter and peaceful development by not just China, Russia, and the U.S., but all nuclear armed states. The second four-year stage, would be more complex, as it would involve bilateral, trilateral, and multi-lateral negotiations among all nine nuclear armed states to address the specific reasons why each of the states possesses nuclear weapons, and to find ways that those incentives could be reduced or eliminated. Intense diplomacy would be required during this period, resulting in all nine nuclear powers joining the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW). The TPNW would give all nine states a ten-year timeline to eliminate their arsenals. However, they could accomplish this in four years, given that the starting point would be arsenals of no more than 600 nuclear warheads. This last four-year stage would involve reductions, verification, and eventual elimination of arsenals. It could be done in plenty of time for the centennial celebration of the United Nations, and the centennial commemoration of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The nuclear age should end well before it turns 100.

 If Reagan and Gorbachev could come so close 40 years ago, we should not rule out the possibility that Putin, Xi, and Trump could do so today. As John Kennedy said in his great American University Commencement Address in 1963, "Our problems are man-made—therefore, they can be solved by man. And man can be as big as he wants. No problem of human destiny is beyond human beings. Man's reason and spirit have often solved the seemingly unsolvable—and we believe they can do it again."
news.summary: TEHRAN, Nov. 18 (MNA) – Presidents Xi, Putin, and Trump should pursue a diplomatic breakthrough in China, with an eye on a nuclear weapons-free world.

news.title: Trump basks in warm welcome of old ally Manila
news.text: MANILA, Philippines — US President Donald Trump basked Wednesday in the warm welcome of reliable ally Manila, part of a whirlwind diplomatic tour that next takes him to talks with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China.Trump, fresh off his Republican party's drubbing in midterm elections, was received by rows of troops and a brass band at the presidential palace as the Philippine segment of his trip neared an end.Since touching down Tuesday, he's met with the so-called Quad security alliance, hailed a coming Thailand trade deal and huddled with leaders from the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations.The US leader also touted an expansion of defense cooperation with Manila and suggested US nuclear technology could help ease the country's energy woes.Marcos in March declared a 'national energy emergency' in the wake of the US-Israel attacks on Iran that led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and sent fuel prices soaring in the import-dependent archipelago.'For the Philippines to embrace American technology in its first modern nuclear project would underscore the strength of the important relationship. And we're going to probably do something very big having to do with nuclear,' Trump said Tuesday, without offering details.Numerous countries, including Japan, Russia, France and South Korea, have been involved in talks aimed at introducing nuclear power to the Philippines for the first time.A kilometer away, about 1,000 protesters chanting 'Trump out' and slogans aimed at the US' Pax Silica AI and rare earths initiative burned US flags after being halted by police on a road leading to the presidential palace.'They were great' Hayley Channer, of the Sydney-based United States Studies Centre, called Trump's decision to stop in Manila en route to Shenzhen 'significant,' telling AFP he had a 'strong personal relationship' with Marcos.At a gala dinner Tuesday evening, Trump praised Marcos's parents as 'great' despite their exile in disgrace after the toppling of Ferdinand Marcos Sr's dictatorship in 1986.'I knew your parents very well, and they were great,' he told a gala dinner of Asean leaders hosted by Marcos on Tuesday. 'You have very good genetics, I can tell you that.'But the two treaty allies also share a raft of security concerns in the Pacific, from Manila's ongoing clashes with China in the disputed South China Sea to the ever-present threat of war over the Philippines' northern neighbor Taiwan.'President Trump sees huge strategic value in the US' relationship with the Philippines, which has been on the front line of China's territorial aggression in the South China Sea,' Channer said.A complex historyThe United States has a long and complex history with the Philippines, a former colonial possession, with the presence of US troops in the Southeast Asian country still a sensitive issue.But under Marcos, access for US troops at Philippine bases has been broadly expanded, joint patrols in the South China Sea have increased, and thousands of troops from both countries work together in large-scale annual exercises.In April, more than 17,000 soldiers, airmen and sailors took part in the 19-day Balikatan, or 'Shoulder to Shoulder,' exercises.Marcos warned in November 2025 that given his country's proximity to the island democracy, 'a war over Taiwan will drag the Philippines, kicking and screaming, into the conflict.'Trump was scheduled to fly Wednesday afternoon to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC), where he will take part in a historic three-way summit with his Russian and Chinese counterparts.Speaking at the Asean summit on Tuesday, he floated potential one-on-one meetings with both Putin and North Korea's Kim Jong Un. Neither has been confirmed.

news.title: Trump Says He Welcomes Foreign Students. His Policies Tell a Different Story.
news.text:
President Donald Trump has repeatedly noted the economic boon from foreign citizens who attend American universities. Yet according to survey results published on Monday, foreign-student enrollment in the U.S. fell substantially this year, largely due to the uncertainty created by Trump's policies.

Based on a survey of more than 800 colleges and universities, the Institute of International Education reported that the number of new foreign students is down 15 percent from last year. Total international enrollment, which fell by 3 percent last year, decreased by 9 percent this year, including drops of 3 percent for undergraduates, 15 percent for graduate students, and 6 percent for participants in optional practical training (OPT).

That two-year decline is "likely historic," Ted Mitchell, president of the American Council on Education, told The New York Times. And according to the survey, the most common explanations offered by institutions that saw reductions were the visa application process, U.S. travel restrictions, "feeling unwelcome in the United States," and limits on the duration of student status.

Foreign students see "too much uncertainty in the United States," NAFSA executive director Fanta Aw, whose organization represents international educators, told the Associated Press. It is not hard to see why.

Last year, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) suddenly terminated thousands of records in the database of foreign students with visas authorizing them to attend American universities. That move, which sowed panic among students across the country, was the result of the Trump administration's "Student Criminal Alien Initiative."

Contrary to the implication of that label, the initiative affected many people who had no criminal convictions that would justify revoking their visas. Nor did ICE cite any other specific justification listed in the relevant regulations. Instead, the students were told their records had been terminated for "otherwise failing to maintain status."

Although ICE subsequently restored the records, they still included notations of the prior terminations. Those black marks, along with the possibility that ICE might reverse course again at any time, left students uncertain about whether they would be allowed to remain in the United States and complete their degrees—a situation that prompted intervention by a federal judge.

Last July, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) finalized a rule imposing a new four-year limit on visas for students, who previously had been allowed to remain in the country until they completed their educational programs, including "authorized practical training following completion of studies." Under the new policy, students who hit the four-year limit, which is inadequate for many courses of study, would have to seek extensions from the DHS, which would have complete, unreviewable discretion to reject such requests.

In September, a federal judge deemed the rule change "arbitrary and capricious" under the Administrative Procedure Act because the DHS did not offer a plausible justification, consider alternatives, estimate predictable costs, or meaningfully respond to the points raised by commenters. U.S. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, a George W. Bush appointee, finalized that judgment on Monday, vacating the rule.

Since the Trump administration can ask a federal appeals court to review Saylor's decision, the ultimate fate of the time limit is unclear. The same goes for the $70,000 OPT application fee that the DHS proposed last month.

All of this is hard to reconcile with what Trump has said about the benefits of hosting international students. "I want to have foreign students," he insisted last year. The full tuition they pay is financially essential to "our school system," he explained.

During his 2024 campaign, Trump agreed that "we need to recruit the best and brightest from the world." In fact, he said, you should "automatically" get a green card when "you graduate from a college." He lamented that people who earned U.S. degrees and "desperately wanted to stay here" ended up returning to their home countries, where they started companies that employ "thousands and thousands of people."

Trump says he welcomes foreign students. His policies tell a different story.

news.title: The Man Who Saved His Family
news.text:
Most people feel closest to those whom they know. Sure, you can tell someone that Thursday is the yahrzeit of his great-great-grandfather, but in the end, he never knew him, and as such, it is hard for him to feel much connection to the deceased. On a Yahrzeit, one generally says the mourner’s prayer (“kaddish”) and may dedicate some Torah learning to the relative’s soul. The custom where I pray in the mornings is to make a small “kiddush” of schnapps and some cake. I always have to keep a bottle of whiskey on hand.

Today (Wednesday) marks the passing of my mother’s uncle. I obviously never knew him, as he passed away many years before I was born. But that does not mean that I am not indebted to him. In a small Jewish section of a Salt Lake City cemetery stands the grave of Moritz Bamberger. He is not to be confused with Utah’s first Jewish governor, Simon Bamberger — apparently of no family connection. I have a picture of Moritz Bamberger’s grave, and the next time we make it back to Utah, I would like to visit. He played no small role in my being part of this world.

When we took things from my parents’ home after their passing, the effort was uneven. I tried to grab any document that might be of familial historical importance. And one thing I brought back to Jerusalem was the last will and testament of Moritz Bamberger. He was born in Wiesenfeld, Germany. He arrived in the U.S. at the turn of the 20th century at age 38. I don’t know his route, but his first known address was in Bonanza City, Custer, Idaho. He was either sent by the family or made his way to make his fortune. His first stop was in a gold-mining town. His next and final home was Salt Lake City, where family lore has it that he did very well in the silver-mining business and ended up owning railroad stocks and other properties. Like with all of my long-gone forefathers, I would have wanted five minutes to ask a dozen questions, but for now all I have is his will.

In it (written in November 1937, immediately prior to his passing), he gives detailed instructions as to the distribution of his wealth. Some is given to charity organizations, both Jewish and more general, like the Neighborhood House. He gave them $200, as well as his clothes and furnishings, to help destitute locals live a better life. The next part of the will has each of 22 recipients receiving 1/40th of the remaining estate after his declared donations, taxes, and expenses. All of those listed were family members in Germany, including my mother and her father (brother of Moritz). He called my mom, his niece, “Elly.” My mother’s name was Ella, and in my life I never heard anyone call her that name. Some of those listed made it out of Germany and arrived in the U.S. Not all did. Another brother, Joseph, was a butcher in Munich. He and his wife were sent to Auschwitz, where they perished. The money set aside by Moritz Bamberger was the financial key to my mother and her parents coming on the S.S. United States at the very end of 1937.

Another document that I have is a sworn statement from Isaac and Frida Heildelberger, who state that they support the arrival of my mother’s family and that the new arrivals should be able to support themselves. But in the event that they could not, they said that they would take financial responsibility (“guarantee to support them as long as it will be found necessary”) for them. This is a far cry from people coming willy-nilly over the border as we had until Donald Trump returned to the White House. One chilling part of their October 1937 letter includes:

“That due to the present conditions in their native country, Germany, they are unable to earn their living there as they are of a Jewish descent.”

One never wants someone to arrive in Israel after substituting U.S., U.K., or France for Nazi Germany referenced in this letter.

The next piece of the puzzle is my grandmother’s naturalization document — with the only picture I have of her — from 1944. In 1954, my grandfather made a will of his own, leaving his bank accounts and belongings to my mother. I never knew either of my maternal grandparents. Again, if I could have five minutes with them…

My mother’s family was like many others that fled Germany and true persecution. Some number of those listed in Moritz Bamberger’s will never made it out. The others arrived and took care of themselves, though they had sponsors who took financial responsibilities so that they would not become wards of the state. If the U.S. stopped giving money at all levels of government to people who are illegally in the country, trillions could be saved. There are only two countries with more than a million Jews: Israel at 7.4 million and the U.S. at 6.3 million. This is no coincidence. These are the two places where Jews feel safest and most comfortable living as accepted citizens free of persecution. Many Jews went through the process described for my family, and a lot of them contributed to the U.S. in every field. Most of the top scientists in the Manhattan Project were refugees from Europe and were grateful for the opportunity to practice their expertise and help the United States win the war. Hyman Rickover said in Congress that his efforts to build the nuclear navy were his way of thanking the U.S. for taking in his immigrant family and granting him admission to the Naval Academy.

Now I’ll save some people time below. Yes, there are Jews whose actions and behavior were not good for the United States. Bernie Madoff, Harvey Weinstein, Jeffrey Epstein are just relatively recent examples. But one can find liars, thieves, criminals, and scoundrels from every religious and ethnic group. That Jews have contributed to virtually every field and area of American life is obvious. Whether it be banking, medicine, science, engineering, and more, one can always find Jews, many being first- or second-generation Americans. When I got into Harvard early, a well-meaning cousin called to implore me that I absolutely had to accept. “You would be the first one in the family to go there!” she intoned. Her parents also fled Germany and actually hosted my father when he did a post-doctoral stint at Columbia. I told her that I was waiting for Princeton. I got in, but the allure of Harvard was too much. When things sucked there during Freshman year, I thought of the quiet, woody campus of Princeton. I got over that when I realized that it was up to me to make the best wherever I was.

Jews have always been grateful for the United States and the freedoms granted. No coincidence that God Bless America was written by none other than Irving Berlin (born Israel Isidore Beilin in Russia). No country is nearly as great, and this Jew is always grateful for the red, white, and blue.
news.author: Alan Joseph Bauer

news.title: Sarah Huckabee Sanders Leads With Clarity and Conviction
news.text:
There's no better time for some good news than the present.

On November 10, Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders released a new book entitled "Unapologetic: Clarity and Conviction in a World Gone Crazy."

Unlike most midterm Republican candidates, Sanders won reelection in a landslide.

I had the opportunity to hear her speak about her new book at the Nixon Library on Veterans Day and was so inspired that I, like others in the room, wondered out loud if she should be on the GOP short list for presidential nominee in 2028.

Her newest book, "Unapologetic," tracks her journey from serving as press secretary in the White House to becoming the first woman elected governor of Arkansas. It gets really personal as she shares the fear she overcame in her battle with cancer that was diagnosed just 60 days before her first election — and the faith that sustained her then and continues to guide her every day.

As she first ran for governor, Sanders addressed issues that she believes matter most to Arkansans: education, lower taxes, jobs, and public safety. And she delivered as a conservative on those issues and was unapologetically pro-life.

Sanders was reelected by a 15-point margin in an election cycle where Republicans suffered crushing losses all across America, including in her neighboring state of Texas.

Every Republican state official on the ballot was elected, along with the entire Arkansas Republican congressional delegation.

While she has supported many of President Donald Trump's policy positions, Sarah expresses a nuanced view on the issue of artificial intelligence (AI). She supports guardrails around AI and opposed a provision in the original version of the One Big Beautiful Bill that would have prevented states from regulating AI. That provision was stripped following objections by her and only a handful of other Republicans.

Her leadership is bold, and as governor of Arkansas, she signed measures limiting youth access to social media, and she expanded school choice options for parents far beyond most states, which I wrote a raving column about months ago.

In her 2023 response to President Joe Biden's State of the Union address, Sanders said Biden was "the first man to surrender his presidency to a woke mob that can't even tell you what a woman is."

She chastised Biden's weak border policies and said her "heart breaks for every parent who has lost a son or daughter to addiction."

She has decried "years of Democrat attacks on law enforcement and calls to defund the police" and policies that "allow violent criminals to roam free, while law-abiding families live in fear."

"Beyond our border, from Afghanistan to Ukraine, from North Korea to Iran, President Biden's weakness puts our nation and the world at risk," Sanders said.

She further criticized Biden's "refusal to stand up to China, our most formidable adversary" as "dangerous and unacceptable."

Sanders issued an Executive Order after Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023, that said, "Hamas terrorists invaded Israel, targeting defenseless families in their homes, killing 1,200 innocent Israelis, and taking 230 hostages, including children and babies." In it, she called out the "shocking rise in antisemitism and pro-Hamas protests in the United States" and said that "These activists deny Israel's fundamental right to defend itself in this war between good and evil."

Sanders speaks, writes, and leads with a clarity and purpose that is refreshing and sorely needed in America today. At the Nixon Library, she invited all the weary in the audience to remember that red-state Arkansas' doors are wide open.

Yet although Sanders is guided by the values of America's heartland and loves her great state of Arkansas, she knows her way around our nation's capital. So if Republicans want to recover from the rebuke voters delivered in this last election, they should take a serious look at the governor of Arkansas who is unapologetically leading with clarity and conviction in a world gone crazy.

Star Parker is the founder of the Center for Urban Renewal and Education and the author of "Necessary Noise, How Donald Trump Inflames the Culture War and Why This Is Good News for America" (Hachette, 2019).

news.title: CBS Champions Book Reviews — by Liberals, for Liberals
news.text:
One of the most ridiculous things that liberal media outlets do is pretend they aren't the slightest bit ideological. Whenever they present their works with a vague sense of objectivity and nonpartisanship, it is remarkably dishonest. But with some viewers, they can absolutely get away with it.

Take the show "CBS News Sunday Morning." On Nov. 15, longtime liberal host Jane Pauley wrapped up the show by talking about book reviews. The Washington Post recently folded its Sunday "Book World" section, and only The New York Times still has a Sunday book-review section. Wherever will we learn from these kinds of nonpartisans about the most thrilling and rollicking anti-Trump books headed for the bestseller list?

CBS doesn't care about a book review section in conservative periodicals like National Review or the Washington Examiner. Those don't count.

Pauley proclaimed: "Bestselling author Jonathan Alter says Book World's closure left a void." He said, "So we stepped into the breach, and we're doing something about it." Pauley added, "Alter is co-founder of The Reader, a new general interest online book review."

The word "liberal" is not applied.

Alter was for many years a perpetually partisan columnist for Newsweek. His most recent books include "His Very Best: Jimmy Carter, a Life" in 2021. Carter was a "global icon," says the promotional copy. "Here is a moral exemplar for our times, a flawed but underrated president of decency and vision who was committed to telling the truth to the American people."

In 2024, Alter's book was "American Reckoning: Inside Trump's Trial -- and My Own." The book blurb is explicit: "As one of a handful of journalists allowed in the courtroom, for 23 days Jonathan Alter sat just feet away from the most dangerous threat to democracy in American history, watching the spectacle of the century: the felony trial of Donald Trump." It came with gassy dust-cover tributes from Stephen Colbert and Lawrence O'Donnell.

Pauley continued with the nonpartisan masquerade bit, noting The Reader will be edited by Haley Sweetland Edwards, who comes over from the liberal hothouse known as Time magazine. "The Reader is part of Washington Monthly, a non-profit magazine," Pauley explained.

The Washington Monthly became well-known as a "neoliberal" magazine that was a farm team for the liberal media, and both Alter and Edwards worked there before they joined Newsweek and Time.

Edwards boasted they would have "mostly book reviews," but also book recommendations from authors like LBJ biographer Robert Caro, Kamala-boosting Ann Patchett and "Handmaid's Tale" propagandist Margaret Atwood. Does that sound non-ideological?

Edwards unsurprisingly gushes, "We have 31 Pulitzer Prize winners who have agreed to be contributors ... the creme de la creme!" The Pulitzer Prizes have become gifts that liberal writers hand to each other.

Then Pauley announced: "And that's where we come in. Each weekend, we'll offer two books for your consideration -- one fiction, one nonfiction -- courtesy of The Reader."

Their first nonfiction pick was "The Sensualist" from "the comedic writer Gary Shteyngart." This Russian-born novelist shows up occasionally to drop bombs on Trump on MS NOW's "The Beat with Ari Melber." Last year, he mumbled about "banned books" under Trump by comparing America to Russia: "Stalin wanted to purge all the, you know, whatever, Mark Twain, et cetera." Say what?

CBS News, under their supposedly "MAGA-friendly" Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss, will now recommend "best books" every week — by liberals, for liberals. As long as no one inside the bubble says "liberal," it's just a service for all people who love books, right? This way, you'll be nudged to expand your mind with books that the liberal commissars recommend to you.
